_comment: Central glossary for the course. Each entry: id, term (display), aliases (extra surface forms to match, case-insensitive), definition (British English, one or two sentences). The app links the FIRST occurrence of each term on a page to a hover/tap tooltip. Keep definitions concise and evergreen.

terms.definition: When an AI generates plausible-sounding but false or unsupported information, stated with the same confidence as fact. It is a structural feature of how language models predict text, not an occasional bug. See Core Module 1.
The working memory of a model — the amount of text (your prompt, the conversation, and any documents) it can consider at once, measured in tokens. Anything outside it is invisible to the model.
The input and instructions you give an AI. The clarity and structure of the prompt strongly shape the quality of the response.
A persistent instruction that defines an AI's role, scope, and behaviour for a whole session — the equivalent of a job description, set before the user's own messages.
Model Context Protocol — an open standard for connecting AI agents to external tools and data sources through a common interface, so the same tool works across different applications.
Producing different outputs from the same input. Language models sample from a probability distribution, so identical prompts can yield varied (though usually similar) responses.
Including a handful of worked examples in a prompt to show the AI the pattern you want, rather than describing it in the abstract. Contrast with zero-shot (no examples).
The unit a model reads and writes — roughly a word fragment of a few characters. Models see text as sequences of tokens, which is why they can stumble on spelling, counting letters, or arithmetic.
The fixed numerical parameters learned during training that encode what a model "knows". They don't change as you chat — only the context does. See Core Module 1 on weights versus context.
An AI system that can take actions, not just produce text: model plus tools plus a loop, where it decides a step, acts, observes the result, and repeats towards a goal. See Core Module 4.
An AI's tendency to agree with you and tell you what you seem to want to hear, rather than what is accurate — a reason to invite disagreement and verify independently.
The uneven boundary of AI capability: it performs brilliantly on some tasks and fails on others of seemingly similar difficulty, with no obvious line between the two. See Core Module 1.
Retrieval-augmented generation — fetching relevant documents and placing them in the context window so the model answers from supplied sources rather than from memory alone.
Further training a base model on additional examples to adapt its behaviour or style. Unlike prompting or context, this changes the model's weights.
A setting that controls randomness in a model's output: lower values make responses more focused and predictable, higher values more varied and creative.
A model trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which in aggregate produces fluent language, reasoning, and knowledge recall. The technology behind tools like Claude and ChatGPT.
